newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - JP Morgan touts new credit risk tool.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - JP Morgan touts new credit risk tool.

text.p: The architect of J.P Morgan & Co's new CreditMetrics system for measuring a bank's credit risk said he hopes it can become a benchmark used to amend the Basle Accord's "one-size-fits-all" approach to the amount of capital banks must hold against credit risk.

"We are not suggesting that this should be THE standard," Stephen Thieke, managing director of J.P. Morgan's Corporate Risk Management Group, told Reuters in a telephone interview. "What we're trying to suggest is that this could be a benchmark...for helping one to better understand and quantify the credit risk that they take."

In his previous job as executive vice president of the New York Fed, Thieke helped draft the capital adequacy norms agreed to at the Bank for International Settlements under the 1988 Basle Accord. The norms call for a capital cushion of at least eight percent against assets weighted according to the risk of obligations not being paid.

Banks have complained the risk weightings given to different credit exposures are unsophisticated, and the formula paints their risk-profile with too broad a brush. It requires the same capital allocation for high-grade corporate debt and leveraged buyout loans. And a well-diversified portfolio needs the same amount of capital as an undiversified one.

"It's time to take a look at what might replace it," said Thieke. The CreditMetrics system, he said, "can show the way to an equivalent approach to looking at credit risk which is more sensitive to the actual risk-profile of a portfolio."

Many banks have constructed their own risk-measuring models for internal use. But most of these, he said, are oriented toward market risk, or the changes in the value of a position in response to market moves.

CreditMetrics focuses instead on quantifying credit risks individually or across a portfolio. It covers a broad spectrum of transactions including traditional loans, fixed income instruments, commercial contracts, and derivative products.

The model, which is backed by Bank of America, BZW, Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, Swiss Bank Corp and Union Bank of Switzerland, takes into account the potential impact of upgrades and downgrades, default probabilities and expected recovery rates, and portfolio concentration.
"To my knowledge, there are no other readily available methodologies for looking at credit risk," Thieke said.

"Efforts like CreditMetrics are a good step forward in terms of the analytic approach to looking at credit risk issues," said a bank official from one of the international banks backing the product, who asked not to be identified. "One can hope that the improvement in credit risk analytics will lead to a review of the capital adequacy guidelines with respect to credit risk," the banker added.
But, he cautioned, "it's still very early days".
Thieke said it would take a while before regulators revise capital adequacy norms, but the need for a new approach was growing more evident.

An indication of this, he said, was the receptivity of regulators to internal models in the area of market risk. The Bank for International Settlements in Switzerland has ruled that banks can use their own models for market risk measurement from next year.

"I think there's a lot of evidence that the supervisory authorities are keenly interested in understanding developments in this area, being supportive of the idea of innovation and enhancements to internal techniques," he said. "At the same time they're not going to jump prematurely and very quickly change their existing practice".

But in the uncharted waters of credit risk management, regulators may be leery of relinquishing controls in the near future. The use of internal models could reduce the capital reserves banks hold, and breed an overdependence on quantitative techniques. Both those factors make regulators uncomfortable.
